title: 22% of headless ERK-inhibited planaria spontaneously repattern weeks later

fields.label: Label
fields.value: 22% of headless ERK-inhibited planaria spontaneously repattern weeks later

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In Dugesia japonica made headless by transient U0126 (ERK/MAP kinase inhibitor) treatment after amputation, 22% of 181 animals followed until death showed sudden repatterning after four or more weeks without any intervention, mostly between 4 and 10 weeks, and 61% of those regained a normal single-headed morphology.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L 2023, The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis › Experimental results on repatterning of planaria

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In headless animals observed from when they were cut until their death (n = 181), 22% showed some form of sudden repatterning even though regeneration had completed and morphogenesis had ceased weeks prior (figure 10b).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L, Bischof J, LaPalme JV, Levin M, “The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis”, Interface focus (2023), doi:10.1098/rsfs.2022.0072; section “Experimental results on repatterning of planaria”. Scope: Dugesia japonica pre-tail fragments treated with 18 μM U0126 for 3 days

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-goals-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables and decision criteria are direct, and the reported cohort is moderately large. The claim is only partially resolvable unless the underlying animal-level observations are openly available or an independent public replication exists.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use animal-level treatment, survival, observation-time, and morphology records to estimate the proportion repatterning after week four, its timing distribution, and the fraction returning to one head. The stated percentages are refuted if reclassification or survival-adjusted estimates materially differ.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Death and unequal follow-up can bias a simple proportion.

Morphological event classification may not have been blinded.

Public animal-level records and videos are not identified in the source text.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The dose, fragment type, follow-up, and phenotype classes are explicit, so a recount would decide the percentages. Those worm-by-worm scores are not in a public table, and the figshare supplement is a supplementary document rather than the scoring sheet. Without that sheet or an independent cohort, the published summary cannot be checked.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score each Dugesia japonica pre-tail fragment treated with 18 μM U0126 for three days, kept individually until death, for any morphology change after four weeks, and among those for return to one head. A recount near 22% of about 181 animals, mostly between four and ten weeks, with about 61% of the changers restoring one head, would confirm the report; a recount far from those fractions, or an independent cohort at the same dose with almost no late change, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Animal-level weekly scores are not deposited; the public record is the summary and figure 10.

The scoring rubric counts fission and dorsal or lateral outgrowths as repatterning, and fission creates a new wound.

Headless animals cannot feed, so late change is confounded with prolonged starvation.
